implementation_notes: typing.NewType is the stdlib realization: the static checker treats the new type as a distinct type that is a subtype of the original, so a raw int or an OrderId fails where a UserId is expected while a UserId still works wherever the original is accepted. Nothing happens at runtime - UserId(x) is the identity function - so the constructor cannot validate; attach validation with Annotated plus a validation library, or use the dataclass variant when the invariant must hold outside the checker. The classic wrapper class is unnecessary for the type-level guarantee alone.
code_sketch:
from typing import NewType

UserId = NewType("UserId", int)
OrderId = NewType("OrderId", int)

def load_user(user_id: UserId) -> str: ...

load_user(UserId(42))   # ok
load_user(42)           # type checker error: int is not UserId
pitfalls: NewType is erased at runtime: no isinstance check, no __init__ validation, UserId(anything) succeeds - trusting the hint as a runtime guarantee is the standard mistake.
The guarantee covers only annotated call sites; untyped modules, Any, casts and # type: ignore silently pass raw values through.
NewType values have no methods of their own, so behaviour (formatting, ordering) must be free functions taking the alias.

variants.name: frozen dataclass wrapper with validation
variants.implementation_notes: When the invariant must hold at runtime, or the value needs behaviour (str, ordering, serialization), a frozen dataclass is a real distinct runtime type with generated __eq__/__hash__ and a __post_init__ hook for validation; slots=True removes the per-instance dict. The cost is one allocation per wrap plus explicit .value unwrapping at every boundary, which is why the static NewType stays the default for pure type-level distinction.
pitfalls: frozen=True blocks attribute assignment but not mutation of a mutable field, so wrap only immutable payloads (or freeze the member).

Dataclass equality is structural and compares across subclasses unless the class is kept final by convention; two wrappers with the same field name are still unequal only because their classes differ.
slots=True requires Python 3.10+ and prevents adding attributes later, so a wrapper that needs cached derived state must keep slots off deliberately.
